stories.headline: WARSH FED HOLDS BUT DOT PLOT TURNS HAWKISH IN FIRST MEETING
stories.body: In Kevin Warsh's debut as chair, the FOMC left the funds rate at 3.50-3.75%, but the new projections showed 9 of 18 officials now pencil in a rate hike before year-end, a sharp shift from the prior easing bias.
stories.explain: The Summary of Economic Projections doesn't set policy, but its median and dispersion anchor expectations. Moving from a cutting bias to a near-even split on hikes repriced the front end almost instantly, lifting the 2Y to ~4.2% and pushing the dollar to a two-month high. The dot plot's signaling power explains why equities sold off Wednesday before today's rebound.

stories.headline: US AND IRAN SIGN INTERIM DEAL, STRAIT OF HORMUZ REOPENS
stories.body: President Trump signed an interim agreement ending the conflict with Iran and lifting the blockade, reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Risk sentiment jumped as the war-risk premium drained out of energy markets.
stories.explain: Roughly a fifth of global oil transits Hormuz, so any closure threat embeds a fear premium in crude. Removing it sent WTI toward $74.62, the lowest since early March, and that disinflationary signal directly offset the Fed's hawkish tone—cheaper energy eases the inflation worry the dots flagged, helping equities recover.

stories.headline: STOCKS ROAR BACK FROM FED SELLOFF, CHIPS LEAD
stories.body: After Wednesday's drop, the rebound was broad: Russell 2000 +2.12%, the Nasdaq-100 +2.48% to 30,406, and the S&P 500 +1.08%. Semiconductors fueled the comeback as falling oil cooled inflation fears.
stories.explain: The single biggest swing factor was real yields versus growth. Lower oil trims expected inflation, which caps long-end yields even as the Fed leans hawkish on the short end—a steepening dynamic that favors duration-sensitive tech. That's why the NDX outran the S&P by more than a full point today.

stories.headline: WTI SLIDES TOWARD $74 ON IRAN PEACE, LOWEST SINCE MARCH
stories.body: WTI crude fell roughly 4% to about $74.62 a barrel, extending its slide as the Hormuz reopening removed supply-disruption risk and traders unwound the geopolitical premium built up during the conflict.
stories.explain: Oil is priced off marginal supply risk as much as physical balances. With the Strait reopening, the market no longer needs to price the tail scenario of a chokepoint shutdown, so the curve flattened and front-month prices fell hardest. Lower crude feeds straight into headline CPI, complicating the hawkish case the Fed just made.

stories.headline: DOLLAR HITS TWO-MONTH HIGH AS RATE-PATH BETS SHIFT UP
stories.body: The dollar index climbed 0.26% to 100.72, its highest since May 2025, as the hawkish dot plot widened the US rate advantage. Gold slipped about 0.7% to roughly $4,209 under the stronger greenback.
stories.explain: Currencies trade on rate differentials and risk appetite. A Fed signaling possible hikes while peers hold steady widens the carry advantage of holding dollars, lifting DXY. The same higher real-rate impulse raises the opportunity cost of non-yielding gold, which is why bullion pulled back despite the day's geopolitical headlines.

stories.headline: PORTAL ERA SETTLES AS NBA DRAFT LOOMS JUNE 23-24
stories.body: With the transfer window closed and the NBA withdrawal deadline past, all of ESPN's top 100 transfers have committed. Defending champ Michigan won its title with an all-transfer starting five, and the draft tips off June 23 in Brooklyn.

stories.headline: KNICKS CROWNED CHAMPS, BRUNSON FINALS MVP; DRAFT NEXT
stories.body: New York won its first title since 1973, beating the Spurs in five. Jalen Brunson was the unanimous Finals MVP at 32.6 points per game. Attention turns to the June 23-24 draft, with a possible Giannis trade seen as the offseason's first domino.

stories.headline: OFFSEASON QUIETS AS MINICAMPS WRAP, ROSTERS SET
stories.body: Mandatory minicamps have concluded and teams are off until late-July training camps. The free-agent pool still holds useful veterans, but most clubs have set rosters after an active March headlined by moves like Kyler Murray to Minnesota.

stories.headline: CAM COLEMAN HEADLINES PORTAL AS RECRUITING RAMPS UP
stories.body: Auburn's Cam Coleman, ranked the top transfer prospect by 247Sports and Rivals, entered the portal as the marquee available name. June 15 opened direct coach contact with 2028 recruits, accelerating the win-now portal cycle.

deepDive.title: The Dot Plot as a Signaling Device
content: Wednesday delivered a paradox: the Fed under new Chair Kevin Warsh did nothing, holding the funds rate at 3.50-3.75%, yet stocks fell sharply. The mover wasn't the decision but a chart—the dot plot, where 9 of 18 officials now project a hike before year-end, a hard turn from the prior easing bias. Then Thursday flipped the script. A US-Iran interim deal reopened the Strait of Hormuz, crude slid toward $74.62, and equities roared back, the Nasdaq-100 climbing 2.48% to 30,406. Same Fed, opposite tape, in 48 hours.

The dot plot is the Summary of Economic Projections' rate chart: each official anonymously marks where they expect policy to sit. It binds no one, yet it moves billions because markets price expected paths, not just today's rate. When the cluster shifts up, traders mark the whole front end higher in real time. That repricing lifted the 2-year toward 4.2% and the 10-year to 4.44%, and pushed the dollar index to 100.72, a two-month high. Gold, which pays no yield, fell about 0.7% as real rates firmed.

Warsh arrives with a long, rules-based, hawkish reputation and skepticism of open-ended balance-sheet expansion, so a hawkish dot shift reads as credible rather than noise—a first meeting is a signaling moment for any new chair. History shows how potent the dots are: in late 2018 a hawkish projection helped trigger a fourth-quarter selloff, and revisions in 2024 whipsawed rate-cut bets repeatedly. The mechanism is reflexive—guidance shapes expectations, expectations move asset prices, and those prices then feed back into the conditions the Fed is forecasting.

Today's rebound exposes the tension Warsh now manages. The hawkish dots warn that inflation could reaccelerate, but the very same week a geopolitical thaw knocked roughly 4% off oil, the most direct input to headline CPI. Cheaper energy undercuts the inflation case the committee just made, which is why duration-sensitive chips led the bounce even with a hawkish Fed. The question for the months ahead: does a disinflationary oil shock force those dots back down, or does the committee hold its hawkish line and let the dollar and front-end yields keep climbing?
